blocks.title: What is this file?
blocks.what: A Service gives a group of Pods a name. It comes from the core v1 API.
blocks.why: This Service skips the shared address, so a lookup returns each Pod’s own address.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the file, because it cannot tell what you want to create.
blocks.comment: What to create: a Service, from the core v1 API

blocks.title: Give it a name
blocks.what: This Service is called web-headless. Its DNS name is built from it.
blocks.why: A different name from the web Service lets you compare the two side by side.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the file, because every object needs a name.
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-headless

blocks.title: No shared address
blocks.what: clusterIP: None makes the Service headless. It gets no address of its own.
blocks.why: Cluster DNS then answers with the address of every matching Pod, so clients can pick one.
blocks.ifRemoved: The Service gets a shared address, like the web Service, and DNS returns only that.
blocks.comment: Headless: no shared address, so DNS returns each Pod
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-headless
spec:
  clusterIP: None

blocks.title: Which Pods?
blocks.what: The selector picks every Pod labelled app: web, the Pods from the Deployment lesson.
blocks.why: DNS lists only Pods that match and are ready. This block makes the file ready to apply.
blocks.ifRemoved: DNS has no Pods to return, so lookups find nothing.
blocks.comment: Return the Pods labelled app: web
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-headless
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: web

blocks.title: Which ports?
blocks.what: The ports list the port the Pods serve on. No traffic passes through the Service itself.
blocks.why: Clients connect straight to a Pod’s address. The ports tell people and tools where to connect.
blocks.ifRemoved: Lookups still work. A headless Service may leave out ports.
blocks.comment: The port the Pods serve on
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-headless
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80

notes.apiVersion: The API group and version that define this kind. Services are in the core v1 API.
notes.kind: The type of object to create. A Service gives a group of Pods a name.
notes.metadata: Details that identify the object, such as its name.
notes.metadata.name: The Service name. Its full DNS name is web-headless.default.svc.cluster.local.
notes.spec: The desired state: which Pods DNS should return, and on which ports.
notes.spec.clusterIP: None, with a capital N, means no shared address. That makes the Service headless.
notes.spec.selector: The labels a Pod must have to be returned by DNS lookups.
notes.spec.selector.app: Return Pods labelled app: web, the Pods from the Deployment lesson.
notes.spec.ports: The ports the Pods serve on. Each list item is one port.
notes.spec.ports[].protocol: The network protocol. TCP is the default and suits web traffic.
notes.spec.ports[].port: The port this Service lists for clients.
notes.spec.ports[].targetPort: The port on the Pods. nginx listens on 80.

questions.question: What does a lookup of web-headless return?
answers: The address of each ready web Pod
questions.explain: clusterIP: None means no shared address. DNS answers with every matching Pod instead.

questions.question: A web Pod is not ready yet. Is its address returned?
answers: No, DNS lists only ready Pods
Only if it has the label twice
questions.explain: Like any Service, a headless one only lists ready Pods.

questions.question: When is a headless Service useful?
answers: When a client must reach one particular Pod, such as a database copy
When you want a public address
questions.explain: Clients get every Pod’s address and choose for themselves. The StatefulSet lesson builds on this.

fix.message: The Service "web-headless" is invalid: spec.clusterIPs[0]: Invalid value: "none": must be a valid IP address, (e.g. 10.9.8.7 or 2001:db8::ffff)
fix.explain: Only None with a capital N means no address. Kubernetes reads none as an address, and it is not a valid one.
fix.fix: Write clusterIP: None, with a capital N.
